strengths: Introduces the MEMR-Seg task and the MR-MedSeg dataset, containing 177K multi-round medical segmentation dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, five interaction scenario types, and nine imaging modalities, which addresses data scarcity in interactive medical segmentation.

Provides a semi-automatic dataset construction pipeline with manual entity selection, GPT-5-based relationship/template generation, and expert screening, along with detailed dataset statistics and scenario coverage.

Proposes MediRound, a baseline that integrates MedSAM, LLaVA-Med, a [SEG] token, reference-round mask cropping, bounding box encoding, and conversation-history encoding for multi-round medical reasoning segmentation.

Introduces the Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) to mitigate error propagation across rounds, with an algorithm, threshold ablation, and per-round performance analysis showing improved multi-round accuracy.

Reports extensive experiments, including comparisons with human-assisted, MLLM-based, SegLLM, and medical segmentation baselines, as well as per-round, vanilla referring segmentation, backbone, and threshold ablations.
The manuscript is generally clear, with informative figures, a dataset overview, and qualitative examples illustrating multi-round behavior.
weaknesses: The MR-MedSeg dialogues are generated through templates and GPT-5/GPT-4 rather than real clinical multi-round interactions; this raises concerns about whether the data genuinely requires entity-level medical reasoning or mainly tests templated dialogue following.

The baseline comparisons in Tables 1 and 2 are likely unfair: methods such as SegLLM, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Qwen3-VL appear not to be fine-tuned on MR-MedSeg, whereas MediRound is trained on it, so the reported gains may reflect training data exposure rather than architectural superiority.

Potential data leakage is not addressed: MR-MedSeg is built from SA-Med2D-20M, and Table 3 evaluates on the SA-Med2D-20M benchmark without reporting split overlap or contamination analysis, making the referring segmentation results unreliable.

The JCM training protocol is underspecified: the paper does not clearly state the supervision, loss functions, or quality labels used to train the Quality Judgment Module and Correction Module while the main MediRound weights are frozen, which limits reproducibility.

Methodological novelty is incremental: MediRound largely combines existing components (MedSAM, LLaVA-Med, [SEG] token, bounding-box encoder) with lightweight MLP-based correction modules, and the core contribution is more dataset/benchmark than a fundamentally new algorithm.

Reproducibility and attribution are problematic: the code/data link is incomplete, the dataset construction relies on GPT-5 despite citing GPT-4, and several future model names (e.g., Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL) do not match the cited references.

The evaluation lacks statistical significance testing, error bars, and detailed failure-mode analysis, and there is no external validation on real clinical multi-round data, no limitations section, and no discussion of societal or deployment implications.
The definition of 'entity-level reasoning' remains vague, and the five relationship categories may be too narrow and template-driven to substantiate the strong reasoning claims.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practically relevant task, MEMR-Seg, extending medical image segmentation to multi-round, entity-level reasoning with clear clinical motivation.

Constructs MR-MedSeg, a large-scale dataset of 177K multi-round medical segmentation dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 medical entities, and 9 imaging modalities, using a semi-automatic pipeline with expert screening; this is a valuable resource for future interactive medical segmentation research.

Proposes MediRound, a well-motivated baseline that combines MedSAM, LLaVA-Med, bounding-box encoding, reference-round cropping, and dialogue history, and introduces a lightweight Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) to mitigate error propagation across rounds.

Provides extensive experiments: comparisons against human-assisted traditional models, MLLM + segmentation pipelines, and SegLLM; per-round analysis, vanilla referring segmentation results, backbone ablations, JCM threshold analysis, and qualitative examples support the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
Training and implementation details are mostly clear, with code/dataset promised, public SA-Med2D-20M as the source, and hardware, optimizer, LoRA rank, and training time reported.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to the newly constructed MR-MedSeg dataset; no independent clinical multi-round benchmark or external validation is provided, so generalization to real-world medical dialogue remains unproven.

Dataset construction relies heavily on GPT-based template generation and manual annotation; the paper does not report inter-annotator agreement, annotation quality metrics, or linguistic diversity analysis, and the repeated mention of GPT-5 while citing GPT-4 should be clarified for reproducibility.

Data splits are not clearly specified at the image level versus conversation level; if images overlap across training/validation/test through different conversations, reported performance may be optimistically biased. This should be explicitly addressed.

The JCM training details and the definition of quality labels for the Quality Judgment Module are not fully described in the main paper; the mechanism may be difficult to reproduce, and inference-time overhead is not quantified.

Baseline comparisons involving human assistance and MLLM + segmentation pipelines may not be fully controlled or optimized, and no statistical significance tests or error bars are reported, making some conclusions less definitive.

Some claims are somewhat overstated: MediRound is competitive among referring segmentation methods but remains well below bbox-input MedSAM and lower than MediSee on cIoU in Table 3; clinical deployment risks and societal impact are not discussed.

strengths: Formalizes a practically motivated problem: multi-round, entity-level reasoning segmentation in medical imaging, where each round's query depends on the mask produced in a previous round. The task framing and Figure 1 make the practical gap of existing single-round text-prompt methods easy to grasp.

Substantial dataset effort: MR-MedSeg is built on the public SA-Med2D-20M and reported as 177K multi-round dialogues over 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories and 9 imaging modalities, with a documented three-stage pipeline (manual entity selection, GPT-assisted relationship/template generation, expert screening) and a code/data release link.

The baseline is a sensible, efficiently trainable assembly of existing parts (MedSAM encoder/decoder, LLaVA-Med-v1.5-Mistral-7B with LoRA, a bounding-box encoder, and a [SEG] token for mask decoding), trained in ~1.5 days on 4 A6000s, which keeps the benchmark accessible to the community.

The Judgment & Correction Mechanism targets a real, well-articulated failure mode (teacher-forced training vs. autoregressive inference on self-produced masks). Table 2 provides a coherent qualitative validation: the JCM gain grows monotonically with round index (e.g., +2.4 cIoU at Round 2 vs. +8.7 at Round 8), consistent with the stated error-accumulation hypothesis.

Reasonably broad empirical coverage: comparisons against human-guided baselines, MLLM+segmentation two-stage pipelines, SegLLM, plus a vanilla referring-segmentation evaluation and backbone/threshold ablations (Tables 1-4, Figure 7).
Qualitative examples (Figure 6) and the single-round results (Table 3) suggest the model retains competitive conventional referring-segmentation ability while adding multi-round behavior.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. Multi-round reasoning segmentation was already introduced by SegLLM [42], and the paper's contribution reduces largely to a domain transfer plus a dataset. The architecture itself is an assembly of off-the-shelf components (MedSAM + LLaVA-Med + LoRA + linear box encoder), and the JCM is a small inference-time MLP pair. The "new task" framing overstates the technical advance.

The dataset's central claim (entity-level *reasoning*) is not validated. Dialogues are produced from roughly 50-80 templates with GPT paraphrasing; there is no statistic on lexical/structural diversity, no comparison against human-written medical multi-round dialogues, no inter-annotator agreement or quantitative quality control despite mentioning three expert inspectors, and no analysis of whether models can solve rounds via template/shortcut matching rather than the intended anatomical/logical inference. For a benchmark paper this is the load-bearing evidence, and it is absent.

The paper's core mechanism is never ablated. The cross-round reference (cropping the referred mask plus its box) is the defining design choice of MediRound, yet there is no experiment removing it or replacing it with text-only history. Without this ablation, the claim that the model performs cross-round entity-level reasoning is not directly demonstrated; the comparison to "MediRound + READ" does not isolate this factor.

No statistical rigor. All numbers are single-run point estimates with no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests, even though several headline comparisons (MediRound 55.8 vs. +JCM 58.4 cIoU; hard-case 38.2 vs. 40.5) are small. The β threshold analysis in Figure 7 likewise shows small, noisy differences across β values, making the chosen β=0.6 look fragile.

The train/inference mismatch is patched rather than solved. Teacher forcing on ground-truth reference masks followed by an inference-time correction module is an ad hoc remedy; standard alternatives (scheduled sampling with predicted masks, iterative/self-refinement training, or end-to-end joint optimization of the correction module) are neither tried nor discussed. The JCM also requires a separate post-hoc training stage whose supervision and data are only deferred to an appendix.

Split protocol is unspecified and poses a leakage risk. With dialogues generated per image, splitting by dialogue rather than by image would place the same images (and the same template instantiations) in both train and test, inflating all reported numbers. The paper never states the split unit.

Overclaiming in the abstract. "Surpassing conventional medical referring segmentation approaches" is not supported by Table 3: MediRound is below MediSee on gIoU (48.3 vs. 50.4) and cIoU (66.3 vs. 70.8), and only marginally above on Dice (62.1 vs. 61.2). Similarly, the multi-round gains are measured largely against weak or mismatched baselines (e.g., BiomedParse at 21.1 Dice under human guidance, unadapted two-stage MLLM pipelines, and SegLLM applied out of domain).

Comparison fairness is questionable. "Human-Thinking + X" baselines conflate human error with model capability, and the MLLM+segmentation pipelines are not tuned for the medical multi-round setting, so the reported 15% average improvement is difficult to attribute to the proposed method rather than to baseline under-adaptation.

Key methodological content is missing from the review copy: JCM training details, per-scenario dataset descriptions and statistics, and the definitions of "regular case" vs. "hard case" (i.e., the turn-count thresholds) are all deferred to an unavailable appendix, hindering reproducibility assessment.

Related work is thin (two short paragraphs) and the dataset's reasoning taxonomy is described only at a high level, so it is hard to judge how the five scenario types differ in difficulty or whether they exhaust realistic clinical multi-round interactions.
Minor but real: the text states "we employ GPT-5 [1]" while reference [1] is the GPT-4 technical report, an inconsistency that also leaves the actual generation model ambiguous.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated new task, Multi-Round Entity-Level Medical Reasoning Segmentation (MEMR-Seg), that extends reasoning segmentation to continuous, cross-round medical dialogues with a clear practical use case (clinicians iteratively refining masks by referring to prior results).

Constructs a large-scale dataset, MR-MedSeg (177K dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 entity categories, 9 imaging modalities), built on SA-Med2D-20M with a documented semi-automatic pipeline (entity selection, relationship generation, template integration) and professional expert screening, which is a substantive community resource.

Proposes a coherent baseline, MediRound, that fuses reference-round mask features, bounding-box/vision features, history text, and current query into an MLLM with a [SEG] token, and demonstrates strong empirical gains over strong baselines (GPT-4o/Gemini-2.5-Pro/Qwen3-VL combined with IMIS-Net or MediSee, and SegLLM), with ~15% average improvement across metrics.

The Judgment & Correction Mechanism (JCM) targets a real and under-addressed problem—error accumulation in chain-like multi-round segmentation—and offers a lightweight, separately-trained quality-judgment/correction module with an IoU-derived soft quality target; results show consistent benefit that grows with the number of rounds (Table 2).

Experimental evidence is thorough: per-round analysis (Table 2), vanilla referring segmentation comparison (Table 3), ablations on vision/MLLM backbone (Table 4), threshold β sensitivity (Figure 7), and reference-mask extraction strategy (Table A).
The limitations section is candid and detailed (single-target per round, long-sequence sensitivity, loss of conversational ability, 2D-only), which appropriately scopes the claims.
weaknesses: The dialogue data are largely template-based (50–80 semantically equivalent templates per scenario) with GPT-based generation; the headline count of '177K conversations' may overstate genuine multi-round reasoning diversity, since variation is primarily linguistic rather than reasoning-driven. The paper does not report human evaluation of dialogue naturalness/realism or statistics on template reuse per image.

Inconsistent attribution of the generation model: the text repeatedly states 'GPT-5-based generation,' while reference [1] is the GPT-4 technical report. This needs clarification to ensure reproducibility and correct attribution.

The JCM gains over the base MediRound are modest (e.g., val overall 55.8/46.5/55.8 → 58.4/49.0/58.9), and the mechanism is post-hoc with frozen weights; the quality-judgment module is trained against GT-IoU-derived scores but must operate on predicted masks at test time, which introduces a training/inference distribution shift analogous to the teacher-forcing issue the paper itself raises.

The novelty is somewhat incremental relative to SegLLM: the core idea (multi-round reasoning segmentation) is adapted to the medical domain, and the primary new contributions are the domain-specific dataset and an engineering-level baseline/JCM, rather than a fundamentally new methodology.

The human-assisted baselines (Human-Thinking + {BiomedParse, MedPLIB, IMIS-Net, MediSee}) are unconventional and their construction is not fully specified; it is unclear how 'human thinking' was operationalized, how consistently it was applied, and whether the comparison is fair or merely illustrative.

Certain evaluation choices raise questions: SegLLM is a natural-image method expected to transfer poorly to medical images, so its underperformance is unsurprising and contributes limited evidence; comparisons would be stronger with a medical-domain multi-round baseline or an oracle reference-mask condition.

Single-entity-per-round and 2D-only constraints are acknowledged, but their impact on practical clinical utility (e.g., multi-lesion workflows) is not quantified, and the model reportedly loses general conversational ability, which may limit interactive usability.

strengths: Introduces a new and practically relevant task, MEMR-Seg, and constructs a large-scale dataset MR-MedSeg (177K multi-round dialogues, ~118K images, 569K masks, 168 categories, 9 modalities) from SA-Med2D-20M, covering five clinically meaningful multi-round interaction scenarios. This is a valuable resource for interactive medical image segmentation.

Proposes a sensible baseline MediRound combining MedSAM with LLaVA-Med, using reference mask crop and bounding box plus conversation history, and a [SEG] token. Experiments show large improvements over prior multi-round/reasoning methods (e.g., SegLLM, GPT-4o/Gemini/Qwen3-VL+segmentation baselines) on the proposed benchmark.

Introduces JCM, a lightweight inference-time confidence/correction mechanism to mitigate error propagation in chain-like multi-round segmentation. Table 2 shows consistent gains across rounds, especially later rounds, and an ablation on threshold beta is provided.

Provides extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations: overall and per-round metrics, hard/regular case splits, vanilla referring segmentation comparison, backbone ablations, and additional interactive cases. Limitations and future work are discussed in the appendix.
Writing and organization are clear, with helpful figures illustrating the task, dataset scenarios, model architecture, and JCM pipeline.
weaknesses: Dataset construction and validation need more rigor. The pipeline relies on 'GPT-5' for relationship/template generation, but no GPT-5 model/API is specified and reference [1] is GPT-4; this raises reproducibility concerns. The manual annotation and inspection process lacks inter-annotator agreement, annotation guidelines, quality-control statistics, and validation of generated dialogues against real clinical conversations.

Potential data leakage/split issue: the dataset is built from SA-Med2D-20M, and splits are reported by conversations/images without clarifying whether the same underlying image can appear across train/val/test. If multiple conversations share an image, the evaluation may be optimistically biased. A unique-image-level split should be reported.

The comparison to MLLM+segmentation baselines uses 'human guidance' and 'human-thinking' but the guidance protocol, prompt templates, and number of human interventions are not described, making fairness and reproducibility unclear. SegLLM is also evaluated zero-shot/without medical fine-tuning, which may understate its potential.

The claim of 'superior performance in both multi-round and single-round medical segmentation' is not fully supported: in Table 3, MediRound's Dice/gIoU/cIoU (62.1/48.3/66.3) are substantially lower than MedSAM (77.7/67.1/81.0) and IMIS-Net (77.0/67.5/87.2) under bbox-input interactive segmentation. The paper should clarify that gains are within referring/reasoning segmentation and discuss the trade-off.

JCM is only evaluated on the proposed MR-MedSeg dataset; no external validation or robustness analysis is provided. The Quality Judgment Module is trained using ground-truth mask IoU as a soft target, but its calibration/accuracy is not reported. There is no ablation separating the quality judgment and correction modules, nor comparison to simpler confidence-based baselines.

Some experimental details are missing: the READ baseline integration is not explained, the exact prompts and training/inference setup for compared MLLM baselines are absent, and the JCM hyperparameters (e.g., MLP architecture, loss weights) are only partly specified. The reported validation conversation count in Table B (1,129) does not match the text (1,270), suggesting minor inconsistency.

As an algorithmic contribution, the core architecture is a relatively straightforward combination of existing models (MedSAM, LLaVA-Med) with LoRA and MLP heads; the novelty is mainly in the task/dataset. The paper could benefit from stronger architectural or reasoning-specific innovations.

strengths: Introduces a clearly motivated and practically relevant task (MEMR-Seg) that targets iterative, cross-round, entity-referenced segmentation in clinical workflows, filling a gap left by single-round referring/grounding segmentation methods.

Delivers a substantial dataset (MR-MedSeg): ~177K multi-round dialogues, 118K images, 569K masks, 168 categories, and 9 imaging modalities, organized around five clinically plausible inter-entity relationship scenarios, with a semi-automatic annotation pipeline and expert screening.

Provides a working baseline (MediRound) that sensibly combines a medical MLLM (LLaVA-Med), a medical segmentation decoder (MedSAM), and a reference-crop/bounding-box encoding scheme, plus ablations on backbones, reference-mask strategies, and the JCM threshold.
Code, dataset, and a demo video are promised for release, which supports reproducibility and downstream benchmarking.
weaknesses: The central performance claim is not well supported by the comparisons: the strongest reported competitors (GPT-4o/Gemini/Qwen + MediSee/IMIS-Net, Human-Thinking + X, and even SegLLM) are used zero-shot or with hand-crafted human assistance rather than being trained/fine-tuned on MR-MedSeg, while MediRound is trained end-to-end on the same distribution. This is an unfair comparison that inflates the apparent margin and undercuts the claim of 'surpassing conventional medical referring segmentation approaches.' At least one comparable MLLM-based segmentation method (e.g., SegLLM, LISA/LISA++) should be fine-tuned on MR-MedSeg as a controlled baseline.

The 'entity-level reasoning' contribution is largely scripted. Dialogues are produced by GPT-5 paraphrasing 50-80 fixed templates over a predefined set of entity relationships, and each scenario type follows a rigid pattern (e.g., round 1 segment organ, round 2 segment lesion in that organ). The evaluation therefore largely measures the ability to follow templated dependency patterns rather than genuine multi-round reasoning, and the strong wording ('reasoning', 'inference') overstates what is actually conditional segmentation given a prior mask.

Novelty is incremental relative to SegLLM (multi-round reasoning segmentation in natural images) and existing reasoning-segmentation work; the main technical delta is domain transfer to medical imaging plus the dataset, and the architecture is an assembly of existing components (LLaVA-Med + MedSAM + LoRA + reference-crop/box encoders).

The Judgement & Correction Mechanism (JCM) is ad-hoc and only modestly effective. It adds ~2.6 Dice over vanilla MediRound, and its quality module is trained with a ground-truth-derived soft target (IoU between prediction and GT), which makes the 'correction' more a learned feature-refinement/confidence estimate than an actual error-correction signal at inference; the naming overstates its role. Figure 7 also shows sensitivity to the threshold beta.

The reported vanilla referring segmentation results (Table 3) show MediRound is only marginally better than the best prior method (62.1 vs 61.2 Dice), suggesting the architecture itself offers little advantage and that most of the reported gains come from training on the new multi-round data.

Validation and test splits are very small (1,270 and 1,273 conversations, roughly 0.7% of the data) relative to the training set, which raises concerns about the reliability and statistical significance of the reported per-round and per-scenario results, especially given the templated data distribution.

There is an explicit train/test mismatch: training uses teacher forcing with ground-truth reference masks while evaluation relies on the model's own (potentially erroneous) prior-round masks. The paper acknowledges this but only mitigates it with the ad-hoc JCM, leaving a real question about the robustness and practical validity of the multi-round pipeline.

Limited qualitative depth and no error analysis on where the model fails on genuinely novel (non-template) phrasing; the appendix limitations (single-entity-per-round, long-sequence fragility, catastrophic loss of conversational ability, 2D-only) further indicate that the system is far from the interactive clinical tool the framing implies.
